passages.t: ‘Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Psalm. A song for the dedication of the temple. Of David” (verse 1). Then thanks: “I will exalt You, O LORD, for You have lifted me up” (verse 1). “O LORD my God, I cried to You for help, and You healed me” (verse 2). “O LORD, You pulled me up from Sheol” (verse 3).

He calls others to join him, with one of the best-known lines in the Psalms: “For His anger is fleeting, but His favor lasts a lifetime. Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning” (verse 5).

Then he tells his story honestly. When life was easy he was proud: “In prosperity I said, ‘I will never be shaken.’” (verse 6). Then trouble came: “When You hid Your face, I was dismayed” (verse 7). So he argued with God for his life: “Will the dust praise You? Will it proclaim Your faithfulness?” (verse 9).

God answered. “You turned my mourning into dancing; You peeled off my sackcloth and clothed me with joy” (verse 11). “O LORD my God, I will give thanks forever” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
This is a song of thanks after an illness that nearly killed him. ‘Pulled me up from Sheol’ means rescued from the edge of death. The book page explains Sheol.

The heading is a puzzle. David did not build the temple; Solomon did. Some think ‘house’ means David's own palace. Others link it with David choosing the place where the temple would stand (1 Chronicles 22:1). Others think the heading records a later use of the psalm, when it was sung at a dedication. These notes leave it open.

Sackcloth was rough cloth, often of goat hair, worn in grief. To ‘peel it off’ and put on joy was to stop mourning and start celebrating. Dancing was part of Israel's public joy.

Notice the honesty of verse 6. He admits that his confidence had been in his good times, not in God.
passages.later:
Jesus promised his grieving friends, “You will grieve, but your grief will turn to joy” (John 16:20), and he said, “Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh” (Luke 6:21).

Paul could call his troubles “light and momentary” only because of what lay beyond them: “an eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17). And Revelation promises the morning that does not end, when “there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain” (Revelation 21:4).
passages.hard:
‘Joy comes in the morning.’ For some people the night has been very long. Does the psalm mean grief should be over by the next day?

No. ‘Night’ and ‘morning’ are pictures. The psalm says that sorrow is not the last word, not that it will be short. Read the note on Psalm 6 on this. If your night has gone on and on, you are not praying wrong, and you need not carry it alone.
passages.asks:
The psalm asks you to remember a time God brought you through, and to say it out loud to others (verse 4). Thanks shared becomes someone else's hope.

And it asks a hard question about verse 6. What did you trust when things were easy? It is wise to answer that before the next hard time comes.
